questions.text: 1. What effect does adding water to the glass have on the pitch of the sound you hear
questions.answer_html: Adding water generally lowers the pitch of a rubbed glass. The moving water adds inertia to the vibration, so the resonant frequency decreases. Compare the same glass at different fill levels.

questions.text: 2. Will the glass vibrate when it is empty Why or why not
questions.answer_html: Yes. A damp finger rubbing the rim can excite the glass itself. The vibrating glass sends sound waves through the air even when the glass is empty.

questions.text: 1. A dog's tail wags 50.0 times in 40.0 s. a What is the frequency of the tail b What is the period of vibration of the tail
questions.answer_html:
1. f = N/Δt = 50.0/40.0 = 1.25 Hz.
  2. T = 1/f = 1/1.25 = 0.800 s.

questions.text: 2. A certain tuning fork makes 7680 vibrations in 30 s. a What is the frequency of the tuning fork b What is the period of vibration of the tuning fork
questions.answer_html:
1. f = 7680/30 = 256 Hz.
  2. T = 1/256 = 3.91 × 10⁻³ s.

questions.text: 3. Tarzan is swinging back and forth on a vine. If each complete swing takes 4.0 s what is the frequency of the swings
questions.answer_html: One complete back-and-forth cycle takes 4.0 s. f = 1/T = 1/4.0 = 0.25 Hz.

questions.text: What is the speed of a sound wave if its frequency is 256 Hz and its wavelength is 1.29 m
1. If waves maintain a constant speed what will happen to their wavelength if the frequency of the waves is a doubled b halved
questions.answer_html:
1. At fixed speed, λ = v/f. Doubling f halves λ.
  2. Halving f doubles λ.

questions.text: 2. What is the frequency of a sound wave if its speed is 340 m/s and its wavelength is 1.70 m
questions.answer_html: f = v/λ = (340 m/s)/(1.70 m) = 200 Hz.

questions.text: 3. Waves of frequency 2.0 Hz are generated at the end of a long steel spring. What is their wavelength if the waves travel along the spring with a speed of 3.0 m/s
questions.answer_html: λ = v/f = (3.0 m/s)/(2.0 Hz) = 1.5 m.

questions.text: 1. In which spring did the transverse waves travel faster – the small diameter spring or the Slinky
questions.answer_html: Use your travel times over a known length. Compute v = distance/time for each spring and compare. Transverse speed increases with tension and decreases with mass per stretched metre. Diameter alone does not determine which spring is faster.

questions.text: 2. In which spring did the longitudinal waves travel faster
questions.answer_html: Compare the travel times of a compression pulse over the same distance, or calculate distance/time for each spring. Longitudinal speed depends on the spring’s effective stiffness and inertia. Use your observations to rank the two springs.

questions.text: 3. Does the amplitude of the waves affect their speed through the spring
questions.answer_html: For small pulses at the same tension and stretch, speed is approximately independent of amplitude. Compare travel times. A very large pulse can alter the stretch and tension.

questions.text: 4. Does spring tension affect wave speed Explain.
questions.answer_html: Greater tension generally gives a faster transverse pulse. For an ideal stretched string, v = √(F/μ), where μ is the mass per unit length. Stretching the spring may change μ as well as the tension.

questions.text: 5. When a wave travels through the medium like the spring does the medium travel or just the disturbance in the medium
questions.answer_html: The disturbance propagates. Each coil moves temporarily about its equilibrium position as the pulse passes. Track one marked coil to separate local motion from pulse motion.

questions.text: 6. When a wave reflects from a fixed end of the medium does a crest reflect as a crest or is it reflected as a trough In other words is the wave inverted
questions.answer_html: At a fixed end the transverse pulse inverts. A crest returns as a trough. At the boundary, the incoming and reflected displacements sum to zero.

questions.text: 1. Does a circular wave travel out at the same speed in all directions How do you know this
questions.answer_html: In still water of uniform depth, a point pulse spreads at the same speed in every direction. A circular front stays centred on the source, so its radius is the same in every direction at a given time.

questions.text: 2. Describe what happens to the wavelength of a water wave when the frequency of the wave increases.
questions.answer_html: Increasing f usually reduces the wavelength in this tank. Compare crest spacing for the same depth. The relation is λ = v/f. Exact inverse proportionality assumes the speed stays constant.

questions.text: 1. What is the source of all wave motion
questions.answer_html: A disturbance starts a wave. A single disturbance can launch a pulse. Repeated vibrations of the source generate a periodic wave.

questions.text: 2. What kind of wave has no amplitude and no frequency
questions.answer_html: The intended comparison is a single pulse, which has no repetition frequency and no periodic wavelength. A pulse does have an amplitude. A displacement amplitude of zero everywhere means there is no disturbance.

questions.text: 3. How many vibrations per second are there from a radio signal from 107.3 MHz
questions.answer_html: 107.3 MHz = 1.073 × 10⁸ Hz, or 107.3 million oscillations per second.

questions.text: 4. What is the period of a wave that has a frequency of 25 Hz
questions.answer_html: T = 1/f = 1/(25 Hz) = 0.040 s.

questions.text: 5. What is the frequency of a wave that has the period of 2.0 s
questions.answer_html: f = 1/T = 1/(2.0 s) = 0.50 Hz.

questions.text: 6. When a salmon fishing boat captain describes waves as being 8 m high what is the approximate amplitude of these waves Explain your answer.
questions.answer_html: If 8 m describes the full trough-to-crest height, the amplitude is approximately 4 m. Amplitude is measured from equilibrium to a crest or trough.

questions.text: 7. What is the frequency of the second hand on a clock
questions.answer_html: One revolution takes 60 s. f = 1/60 s = 0.0167 Hz.

questions.text: 8. What is the frequency of the hour hand on a clock
questions.answer_html: One revolution takes 12 h = 43 200 s. f = 1/43 200 s = 2.31 × 10⁻⁵ Hz.

questions.text: 9. If the frequency of a sound is tripled what will happen to the period of the sound waves
questions.answer_html: T = 1/f. Tripling the frequency makes the period one-third of its original value.

questions.text: 10. A student measures the speed of water waves in her tank to be 25 cm/s. If the wavelength is 2.5 cm what is the frequency of the waves
questions.answer_html: f = v/λ = (25 cm/s)/(2.5 cm) = 10 Hz. The centimetres cancel.

questions.text: 11. Some microwaves have a frequency of 3.0 × 10¹⁰ Hz. How long is a microwave of this frequency Microwave radiation travels at the speed of light.
12. While fishing a girl notices the wave crests passing her bob once every 6 s. She thinks the distance between crests is about 12 m. What is the speed of the water waves
questions.answer_html: Successive crests arrive 6 s apart, so T = 6 s. v = λ/T ≈ 12/6 = 2 m/s.

questions.label: Warm-up
questions.text: You and a friend both throw rocks into a lake. The rocks enter the water 1.0 m apart. If you were looking down from above draw what you think the wave pattern for each of the rocks will look like. Place the letter X at the point or points where the waves would be the highest.
questions.answer_html: Draw concentric crests around each splash. Mark X at intersections of two crest circles, where the upward displacements add. For simultaneous identical splashes, locations equally distant from both sources receive matching parts of the two ripples at the same time.

questions.label: Conclusion
questions.text: Can you reflect a wave completely Explain your answer.
questions.answer_html: A rigid, lossless barrier that transmits no energy can reflect all incident energy in an ideal model. A real barrier can absorb, transmit, or scatter some energy, and a finite barrier lets waves pass around its ends. Reflected circular fronts appear to come from the mirror-image source behind a flat barrier.

questions.text: 1. When straight waves strike a straight barrier how does the angle of incidence compare with the angle of reflection
questions.answer_html: θᵢ = θᵣ. Measure both ray angles from the normal. The angles between the wavefronts and the barrier are equal as well.

questions.text: 2. When the waves reflect from the barrier does their speed change Does their frequency change Does their wavelength change
questions.answer_html: The reflected waves remain in the same water at the same depth. Their speed, frequency, and wavelength stay the same in the ideal model. Amplitude can decrease.

questions.text: Questions 1. Describe what happens to straight waves when they reflect from a parabolic reflector. Are parabolic reflectors ever used to reflect a light b sound Give examples.
questions.answer_html: Plane waves arriving along the axis reflect and converge toward the focus. A parabolic reflector can concentrate wave energy near that point.

questions.text: 2. Describe what happens when circular waves originating at the focus of a parabolic mirror reflect from the mirror. Name a device that does this with light waves.
questions.answer_html: Waves spreading from the focus leave the ideal reflector as approximately straight, parallel wavefronts travelling along the axis. This reverses the focusing process.

questions.text: 1. What happens to the speed of water waves when the waves pass from deeper water into shallower water
questions.answer_html: In the ripple-tank model the waves slow down in shallower water, as shown by closer crest spacing at the same frequency.

questions.text: 2. You did not actually measure the wave speeds. How did you know the speeds had changed and by how much they had changed
questions.answer_html: Use v = fλ and constant f. The ratio v(shallow)/v(deep) = λ(shallow)/λ(deep). Measure several crest spacings in each region and divide by the number of intervals before taking the ratio.

questions.text: 3. Why can you assume the wave frequency is constant as the waves proceed across the water in your wave tank
questions.answer_html: The generator fixes the number of crests per second. At a stationary boundary each incident cycle drives one transmitted cycle, so the frequency stays constant.

questions.text: 4. When water waves enter shallow water in a direction such that the waves are parallel to the boundary does the direction of the waves change
questions.answer_html: If the fronts are parallel to the boundary, the direction of travel is along the normal. The waves continue straight while slowing and shortening their wavelength.

questions.text: 5. When water waves enter shallow water from deep water in such a direction that the waves form an angle greater than 0° with the boundary does their direction change If so in what way does it change Is the angle of refraction greater than equal to or less than the angle of incidence
questions.answer_html: At oblique incidence the ray bends toward the normal as it enters slower, shallow water. The refraction angle is smaller than the incidence angle. Equivalently, the transmitted crests make a smaller angle to the boundary.

questions.text: 6. When water waves leave shallow water and return to deep water how does their direction change For the water waves leaving the shallow water how does the angle of refraction compare with the angle of incidence for the water waves that were coming into the shallow water in the first place
questions.answer_html: On returning to faster deep water, the ray bends away from the normal. If the two boundaries are parallel and the outer depths match, the final ray is parallel to the original. The exit refraction angle then equals the original incidence angle.

questions.text: 1. Is diffraction more noticeable with short wavelengths or long wavelengths
questions.answer_html: For a fixed gap or obstacle, diffraction is more noticeable with longer wavelengths. Compare wavelength with the size of the feature.

questions.text: 2. Is diffraction more noticeable with small openings or large openings
questions.answer_html: For fixed wavelength, smaller openings give broader spreading when the opening is comparable to or smaller than λ. A very small opening can transmit less energy.

questions.text: 3. When straight waves pass through a small opening what shape do the diffracted waves have Sketch a diagram.
questions.answer_html: Draw nearly semicircular wavefronts centred on the opening. The gap acts roughly like a point source when it is narrow compared with the wavelength.

questions.text: 4. When straight waves pass by a small obstacle what happens to the straight waves if the obstacle is a very small compared with the wavelength of the waves b about the same size as the wavelength c very large compared with the wavelength
questions.answer_html:
1. If the obstacle is very small relative to λ, the wave wraps around it with little persistent shadow.
  2. If its width is comparable to λ, the fronts curve appreciably around both edges.
  3. If the obstacle is much larger than λ, a clear shadow forms behind it, with some spreading at the edges.

questions.text: 5. Describe at least three examples of situations you encounter daily that involve diffraction of waves of one sort or another. These might involve water waves sound or light.
questions.answer_html: Examples include hearing someone around a corner, seeing ripples spread around a pier, and seeing a starburst when viewing a streetlight through fine mesh.

questions.text: 1. When the two pulses pass through each other such that a crest passes through a crest as would happen in Figure 6.2.14 a what happens to the amplitude of the combined waves
questions.answer_html: The displacements add. Equal crests of height A give a combined crest of 2A during exact overlap.

questions.text: 2. When a crest arrives at the same point as a trough as would happen in Figure 6.2.14 b what happens to the amplitude of the combined waves
questions.answer_html: Equal and opposite displacements add to zero where they coincide. The original pulses continue after they pass through each other.

questions.text: 1. When crests from one wave source arrive simultaneously with troughs from another wave source what will you see on the screen at that point Why
questions.answer_html: For equal amplitudes, a crest and trough cancel. The screen loses the alternating bright/dark crest pattern there, leaving a relatively steady region or nodal line.

questions.text: 2. When crests arrive with crests and troughs with troughs from two different wave sources what will you see at that spot on the screen Why
questions.answer_html: Crests add to crests, and troughs add to troughs. The displacement is larger and the projected pattern shows stronger variation at this maximum.

questions.text: 3. Regions of zero disturbances on the screen appear as nearly straight lines called nodal lines. If a point on such a nodal line was a distance of nλ from one point source of waves where λ is the wavelength and n is an integer how far would the same point be from the other point source Is there more than one answer to this question
questions.answer_html: The second distance must be a half-integer multiple of λ, such as (n ± ½)λ. In general the absolute path difference is (m + ½)λ for m = 0, 1, 2, …. Several distances are possible if the geometry allows them.

questions.text: 4. Regions of maximum disturbance on the screen sometimes called maxima occur when the distance from one source is for example mλ where m is an integer and λ is the wavelength. What is the distance to the other source Is there more than one possible answer Explain.
questions.answer_html: The second distance can be any integer multiple of λ allowed by the geometry, including mλ itself. The path difference must be an integer multiple of λ, including zero.

questions.text: Complete these diagrams to show what happens to waves after they encounter the barrier or other obstacle. Name the phenomenon that occurs in each situation. 1. source solid barrier phenomenon. Circular wavefronts spread from a point toward a solid vertical barrier.
questions.answer_html: Reflection. Put a virtual source the same distance behind the barrier as the real source is in front. Draw reflected circular arcs on the incident side of the barrier, centred on that virtual source.

questions.text: Complete these diagrams to show what happens to waves after they encounter the barrier or other obstacle. Name the phenomenon that occurs in each situation. 2. phenomenon. Straight, vertical wavefronts move right toward a narrow gap in a barrier.
questions.answer_html: Diffraction. Leave the straight incident fronts on the left. Draw spreading semicircular fronts centred on the narrow gap on the right.

questions.text: 3. If you look at streetlights through a fine mesh curtain you will see a istarburstw effect. What phenomenon is involved in this situation phenomenon
questions.answer_html: Diffraction. The closely spaced threads act like a two-dimensional grating, spreading light into directions that can produce the starburst pattern.

questions.text: 4. Use the following diagram to answer the questions below. deep shallow a The diagram shows water waves in a wave tank moving from deep water into shallow water and then back into deep water. What property of waves does this model illustrate b According to the diagram what can you conclude happens to the waves when they enter the shallow water deep. The fronts pass through a strip of shallow water between two deep-water regions. Their spacing and slant change within the strip.
questions.answer_html:
1. Refraction at each boundary.
  2. In shallow water the crest spacing is smaller, so λ and v decrease at fixed f. The fronts turn. At the parallel exit boundary they turn back to their original orientation if the two deep-water speeds are equal.

questions.text: 5. For the following situations is there a point where the amplitude will be zero everywhere If so mark that point. a b c d e f. The approaching pairs are (a) equal crests, (b) unequal crests, (c) an equal crest and trough, (d) an unequal crest and trough, (e) tall then short crests facing shallow then deep troughs, and (f) tall then short crests facing deep then shallow troughs.
questions.answer_html:
1. No. Like-signed equal pulses add.
  2. No. The pulses have the same sign and unequal amplitudes.
  3. Yes. Mark the midpoint where the centres meet. Equal and opposite profiles sum to zero at exact overlap.
  4. No. Opposite signs alone are insufficient because the amplitudes differ.
  5. No. The two lobes arrive in opposite spatial order, so the profiles cannot cancel everywhere simultaneously.
  6. Yes. Mark the overlap location. The tall crest aligns with the deep trough and the shorter crest aligns with the shallower trough.

questions.text: 6. For which of the following waves can wave interference occur _____ sound _____ light _____ water
questions.answer_html: All three can interfere. Sound pressure, the electric field of light, and water-surface displacement can each superpose.

questions.text: 7. For which of the following waves can the Doppler effect occur _____ sound _____ light _____ water
questions.answer_html: All three can exhibit a Doppler shift in measured frequency when source and observer move relative to each other along the line of travel. For waves in a medium, source and observer motion are measured relative to the medium.

questions.text: 8. Does the Doppler effect occur if you are moving and the object making the noise is stationary Explain your answer.
questions.answer_html: Yes. Moving toward a stationary source makes you encounter the wavefronts more often. Moving away makes you encounter them less often.

questions.text: 9. What can you conclude about the speed of an airplane overhead if you hear a sonic boom
questions.answer_html: The aircraft was supersonic when it generated the shock that reached you. The shock travels outward and can reach the ground after the aircraft has passed.

questions.text: 10. What is the difference between a sonic boom and the sound barrier
questions.answer_html: The sound barrier refers to the aerodynamic effects near Mach 1, including compression and shock formation. A sonic boom is the sound heard when a shock from supersonic motion passes an observer.

questions.text: 11. Draw two waves travelling toward each other that will create destructive interference when they meet.
1. What is the difference between a pulse and periodic waves
questions.answer_html: A pulse is a single travelling disturbance. A periodic wave repeats regularly in time because the source repeats its motion.

questions.text: 2. Explain with the help of a sketch what each of these terms means with respect to waves: a crest b trough c wavelength d frequency e amplitude
questions.answer_html:
1. A crest is a point of maximum upward displacement.
  2. A trough is a point of maximum downward displacement.
  3. Wavelength is the distance between successive points at the same phase, such as crest to crest.
  4. Frequency is the number of complete oscillations per second at a point.
  5. Amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium.

questions.text: 3. What is a hertz
questions.answer_html: 1 Hz = one cycle per second = 1 s⁻¹.

questions.text: 4. How are frequency and period related
questions.answer_html: Frequency and period are reciprocals. f = 1/T and T = 1/f.

questions.text: 5. A dog wags its tail 50 times in 20 s. What are a the frequency and b the period of vibration of the tail
questions.answer_html:
1. f = 50/20 = 2.5 Hz.
  2. T = 1/2.5 = 0.40 s.

questions.text: 6. What is the difference between a transverse wave and a longitudinal wave
questions.answer_html: For a transverse wave, the oscillation is perpendicular to the wave’s travel direction. For a longitudinal wave, it is parallel.

questions.text: 7. For any kind of wave motion how are wave speed wavelength and frequency related to one another
questions.answer_html: v = fλ. A crest travels one wavelength in one period, so v = λ/T.

questions.text: 8. Alternating current in power lines produces electromagnetic waves of frequency 60 Hz that travel outward at the speed of light which is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. What is the wavelength of these waves
questions.answer_html: λ = c/f = (3.0 × 10⁸)/60 = 5.0 × 10⁶ m, or about 5000 km.

questions.text: 9. If the speed of sound is 330 m/s what wavelength does a sound of frequency 512 Hz have
questions.answer_html: λ = v/f = 330/512 ≈ 0.645 m (about 0.64 m).

questions.text: 11. Explain the difference between refraction and diffraction. Give an example of each phenomenon from everyday experience.
questions.answer_html: Refraction is a change in direction as wave speed changes, as when an oblique light ray enters water. Diffraction is spreading around edges or through an opening, as when you hear a voice around a corner.

questions.text: 12. When waves slow down on entering a new medium what happens to a their wavelength b their frequency c their direction d Under what conditions will the direction not change
questions.answer_html:
1. The wavelength decreases because λ = v/f.
  2. The frequency stays the same at a stationary boundary.
  3. At oblique incidence the slower wave bends toward the normal.
  4. At normal incidence the propagation direction is unchanged.

questions.text: 13. a What is constructive interference b What is destructive interference
questions.answer_html:
1. Constructive interference occurs when displacements reinforce, such as two crests meeting.
  2. Destructive interference occurs when opposite displacements reduce the sum. Equal and opposite displacements cancel completely.

questions.text: 14. In a wave tank what causes a nodal line A maximum
questions.answer_html: For two coherent, in-phase sources of equal amplitude, a nodal line forms where the path difference is (m + ½)λ. A maximum occurs where the difference is mλ, including zero. Here m is a nonnegative integer.

questions.text: 15. The following diagram shows two parabolic reflectors. A small source of infrared heat is placed at the focus of one of the mirrors. Soon after a match at the focus of the other reflector lights on fire. Draw a diagram showing how the wave model explains this. f matchhead source of infared radiation f
questions.answer_html: The first mirror sends radiation from its focus into a nearly parallel beam. The facing mirror collects that beam and concentrates it at its focus, where the match absorbs energy.

questions.text: 16. The sonar on a Canadian navy submarine produces ultrasonic waves at a frequency of 2.2 MHz and a wavelength of 5.10 × 10⁻⁴ m. If a sonar technician sends one wave pulse from underneath the submarine toward the bottom of the ocean floor and it takes 8.0 s to return how deep is the ocean at this point
questions.answer_html: v = fλ = (2.2 × 10⁶)(5.10 × 10⁻⁴) = 1122 m/s. The pulse travels down and back, so depth = vΔt/2 = (1122)(8.0)/2 ≈ 4.5 × 10³ m, measured below the submarine.

questions.text: 1. Label the trough crest amplitude and wavelength on the image below. The image shows a repeating wave crossing a horizontal equilibrium line.
questions.answer_html: Label a highest point crest and a lowest point trough. Mark amplitude vertically from the midline to a crest. Mark wavelength horizontally between adjacent crests or adjacent troughs.

questions.text: 2. If a wave from trough to crest is 4.2 m high what is the amplitude of the wave
questions.answer_html: A is half the trough-to-crest height. A = 4.2/2 = 2.1 m.

questions.text: 3. At room temperature sound has a speed of 3.4 × 10² m/s. What is the wavelength of sound from a tuning fork that vibrates at 256 Hz
4. Light travels with a speed of 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s. What is the frequency of red light if its wavelength is 610 nm 1 nm = 1 nanometre = 10⁻⁹ m
5. A rubber duck is floating in the waves and goes up and down three times in 1 s. If the wave travels an average distance of 4 m in a second what is the wavelength
questions.answer_html: f = 3 Hz and v = 4 m/s. λ = v/f = 4/3 ≈ 1.3 m.

questions.text: 6. What is the frequency of a wave that has a period of a 100 s b 0.5 s c 1.0 × 10⁻² s
questions.answer_html:
1. f = 1/(100 s) = 0.010 Hz.
  2. f = 1/(0.5 s) = 2 Hz.
  3. f = 1/(1.0 × 10⁻² s) = 1.0 × 10² Hz.

questions.text: 7. In the diagram below which wave has a the longest period b the lowest frequency c the highest frequency 1 2 3 4. The four rows show progressively more complete cycles over the same horizontal span.
questions.answer_html:
1. Wave 1 has the longest period.
  2. Wave 1 has the lowest frequency.
  3. Wave 4 has the highest frequency.

These comparisons assume the diagrams use a common time axis or show spatial snapshots of waves travelling at the same speed. Spatial spacing by itself gives wavelength.

questions.text: 8. What is the period of the hour hand on a clock
questions.answer_html: One revolution takes 12 h = 43 200 s.

questions.text: 9. What is the period of the second hand on a clock
questions.answer_html: One revolution takes 60 s.

questions.text: 10. An observer counts 36 waves arriving at the shore of a beach in a time of 3.00 min. a What is the frequency of the waves b What is the period of the waves
questions.answer_html:
1. 3.00 min = 180 s. f = 36/180 = 0.200 Hz.
  2. T = 1/f = 5.00 s.

questions.text: 11. A small spider has became lost while looking for its web site. The spider is on the surface of an old phonograph record which is spinning at 33 rpm rotations per minute . It is trying to escape by jumping on the needle of the phonograph player. The spider misses the needle on the first try. How long will it have to wait for the next try
questions.answer_html: The spider returns to the needle’s position after one revolution. T = (60 s)/33 ≈ 1.8 s.

questions.text: 12. If you increase the frequency of the wave generator in a wave tank what happens to the wavelength of the waves
questions.answer_html: Wavelength decreases when the source frequency increases, assuming the same wave speed. If speed is approximately constant, λ is inversely proportional to f.

questions.text: 13. What is the wavelength of a wave that has a frequency of 34 Hz and is travelling at 2.5 m/s
questions.answer_html: λ = v/f = 2.5/34 ≈ 0.074 m = 7.4 cm.

questions.text: 14. What is the frequency of a wave that has a wavelength of 25 cm and is travelling at 5 km/h
questions.answer_html: 25 cm = 0.25 m and 5 km/h = 5/3.6 m/s ≈ 1.39 m/s. f = 1.39/0.25 ≈ 5.6 Hz before rounding to the precision of the given speed.

questions.text: 15. What is the speed of a sound wave with a frequency of 200 Hz and a wavelength of 35 m
questions.answer_html: v = fλ = (200)(35) = 7.0 × 10³ m/s from the given data. This is far above the speed of sound in room-temperature air.

questions.text: 16. A helicopter pilot with nothing better to do counts 250 crests of water waves in a distance of 100 m on a lake below him. What is the wavelength of the waves
questions.answer_html: Using 250 wavelengths across 100 m gives λ ≈ 100/250 = 0.40 m. If 100 m is measured from the first crest to the 250th crest, use 249 intervals and get 0.402 m, which also rounds to 0.40 m.

questions.text: 17. The speed of light is 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s. What is the frequency of light waves if their wavelength is 600 nm 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m Consult a spectrum chart to see what colour of light this would be.
questions.answer_html: 600 nm = 6.00 × 10⁻⁷ m. f = (3.0 × 10⁸)/(6.00 × 10⁻⁷) = 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. A wavelength of 600 nm is approximately orange.

questions.text: 18. What measurable property of waves does not change as the waves move from one medium into another
questions.answer_html: Frequency stays the same across a stationary boundary, so the period also stays the same. Speed, wavelength, and amplitude can change.

questions.text: 19. Draw two waves travelling toward each other that will create constructive interference when they meet.
